newsitem.title: USA: U.S. backs new Northern Ireland talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. backs new Northern Ireland talks.

text.p: Amid speculation the talks may fold permanently, the United States on Monday renewed its strong support for Northern Ireland peace negotiations and pleaded again with the IRA to observe a ceasefire.
"The United States strongly supports the Northern Ireland peace process, which will face challenges in the weeks ahead," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

In addition to substantive issues that remain to be decided, "those opposed to the talks continue to mount acts of violence, which are designed to poison the atmosphere and to scuttle these talks," he said.

Burns said "a decision by the Irish Republican Army to forswear violence and terrorism, and to help implement a lasting ceasefire would contribute immeasurably to the ongoing efforts led by the British and Irish governments to end the conflict in Northern Ireland. And the United States again urges the IRA to take these steps."
The talks were to reconvene this week in Belfast under the chairmanship of U.S. envoy George Mitchell. The last session was held in late December.
British and Irish officials on Sunday denied media speculation that troubled multi-party talks on British-ruled Northern Ireland may soon fold permanently.

But worsening guerrilla violence, pre-election rivalry between British political parties and uncertainty over whether pro-British Loyalist parties will be expelled from the talks for links with guerrilla groups have caused a logjam.
The London-based Sunday Times reported that the talks, which have limped along since June, would be suspended within four weeks to allow the region's parties to prepare for the election.
Officials in London, Dublin and Washington warned that the ailing peace process may never be resumed, the newspaper said.
It quoted American sources as saying Mitchell was "disillusioned by lack of progress and failure to secure a new IRA (Irish Republican Army) ceasefire."
